plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single labeled diagram of an upward-opening parabola drawn on a Cartesian coordinate plane, with thin black arrowed axes crossing near the lower left of the curve and marked x at the right and y at the top. The parabola is a heavy dark blue curve whose two branches end in arrowheads pointing up and outward. Its lowest point is a filled dark blue dot above the horizontal x-axis, connected by a short leader line to the label Vertex at the left. A dashed orange vertical line rises through that dot and carries the orange label Axis of symmetry at the upper right. Directly above the vertex on that same vertical line sits a small teal dot labeled Focus in teal. A short dashed blue horizontal segment runs through the teal dot from one branch of the curve to the other and is tagged Latus rectum by a curved arrow from the upper left. Below the vertex, a dashed red horizontal line spanning the width of the frame is labeled Directrix in red, and the x-axis lies lower in the frame. Color-coding the four named features separately lets the reader see that the axis of symmetry meets the directrix at a right angle and that the vertex lies midway between focus and directrix. The drawing establishes the vocabulary used to define a parabola as the set of points equally distant from the focus and the directrix.

interactionPlan.concept: A parabola is defined geometrically as the set of all points equidistant from a fixed point (the focus) and a fixed line (the directrix).
elements: x-axis (horizontal black line with arrowheads at both ends, labeled 'x')
y-axis (vertical black line with arrowheads at both ends, labeled 'y')
Parabola curve (thick dark blue upward-opening curve, ending in arrowheads)
Vertex (filled dark blue dot at the lowest point of the parabola, with label 'Vertex' and leader line)
Focus (filled teal dot above the vertex, with teal label 'Focus')
Directrix (dashed red horizontal line below the vertex, with red label 'Directrix')
Axis of symmetry (dashed orange vertical line passing through vertex and focus, with orange label 'Axis of symmetry')
Latus rectum (dashed blue horizontal line segment passing through the focus and ending on the parabola, with label 'Latus rectum' and curved leader arrow)

Distance construction lines (only visible in 'Distance definition' view: a sample point on the parabola, a segment from focus to sample point, and a perpendicular segment from sample point to directrix, both marked with equality ticks)

interactions.label: Focal length (p)
interactions.teaches: The distance p from the vertex to the focus (and directrix) strictly controls curvature; increasing p pushes the focus and directrix apart, causing the parabola to widen proportionally.

interactions.label: Display mode
interactions.teaches: Beyond being a U-shaped curve, every single point on a parabola maintains an exact 1:1 distance ratio between the focus and the directrix.
Each term (vertex, focus, directrix, axis of symmetry, latus rectum) isolates a specific structural component of the parabola's anatomy.

demo_steps.title: Anatomy of a parabola
demo_steps.narration: A parabola is built around its axis of symmetry. The vertex sits exactly halfway between the focus above it and the directrix below it.

demo_steps.title: Changing the focal length
demo_steps.narration: Drag the slider to increase the focal length p. As the focus and directrix move further from the vertex, the parabola widens. The latus rectum width is always 4 times this distance p.

demo_steps.title: The geometric definition
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the distance definition. If you pick any point on the curve, its distance to the focus is perfectly equal to its straight-line distance down to the directrix.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The shape of a parabola is not arbitrary; it is the precise geometric path created by maintaining equal distance between a single point (the focus) and a single line (the directrix).
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Place the origin near the lower-left so the parabola occupies the first quadrant. Use the specific colors requested: dark blue curve and vertex, teal focus, red dashed directrix, orange dashed axis of symmetry, light blue dashed latus rectum. In 'Vocabulary' mode, show all terms with subtle leader lines. In 'Distance definition' mode, fade out the latus rectum and axis of symmetry labels, and introduce a sample point on the curve with equal-length segments connecting it to the focus and straight down to the directrix, labeled with equality tick marks.

authoredContext:
In Quadratic Functions, we learned about a parabola’s vertex and axis of symmetry. Now we extend the discussion to include other key features of the parabola. See the figure. Notice that the axis of symmetry passes through the focus and vertex and is perpendicular to the directrix. The vertex is the midpoint between the directrix and the focus.

The line segment that passes through the focus and is parallel to the directrix is called the latus rectum. The endpoints of the latus rectum lie on the curve. By definition, the distance d from the focus to any point P on the parabola is equal to the distance from P to the directrix.

Key features of the parabola

This image displays a parabola on a Cartesian coordinate plane, clearly labeling its fundamental geometric elements. The blue curve represents the parabola itself. The "Vertex" is indicated as the turning point of the parabola. Inside the curve, the "Focus" is marked, a critical point for defining the parabola. A dashed orange line, labeled "Axis of symmetry", passes vertically through both the vertex and the focus. Below the vertex, a horizontal dashed red line shows the "Directrix". Finally, a horizontal dashed blue line segment passing through the focus and extending to the parabola is identified as the "Latus rectum".

To work with parabolas in the coordinate plane, we consider two cases: those with a vertex at the origin and those with a vertex at a point other than the origin. We begin with the former.
